# Antithyroid drugs

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Relevant pharmacology > Antithyroid drugs*

[Original Article Link](/library/Fm0ghg)

---

## Summary

Antithyroid drugs are drugs that either decrease <u>thyroid hormone synthesis</u> (<u>thionamides</u>) or <u>thyroid hormone</u> release (iodides). The most important group of antithyroid drugs are <u>thionamides</u>, which include <u>methimazole</u>, <u>carbimazole</u>, and <u>propylthiouracil</u>. <u>Thionamides</u> decrease <u>thyroid hormone synthesis</u> by inhibiting <u>thyroid peroxidase</u>, an essential enzyme involved in multiple steps of <u>thyroid hormone synthesis</u>. <u>Thionamides</u> play a significant role in the <u>treatment of hyperthyroidism</u> and <u>thyroid storm</u>. Iodides are solutions containing <u>potassium iodide</u> that inhibit the release of <u>thyroid hormones</u> into the circulation. They are, therefore, a useful adjunct treatment in the <u>management of thyroid storm</u>, but their main clinical use is for the <u>preoperative preparation</u> of a patient with <u>Graves' disease</u>, because they decrease the vascularity of the <u>thyroid gland</u>.

---

## Overview

| Overview of antithyroid drugs |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Thionamides | Potassium iodides |
| Examples | <br><br>* Methimazole<br><br>* Carbimazole<br><br>* Propylthiouracil<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Lugol's iodine (oral <u>potassium iodide</u>)<br><br>* Saturated solution of potassium iodide (<u>SSKI</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Mechanism of action | <br><br>* Inhibits <u>thyroid hormone production</u> via inhibition of <u>thyroid peroxidase</u> → blockade of iodide oxidation, organification, coupling<br><br>* <u>Propylthiouracil</u> also lowers peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 by inhibiting <u>5'-deiodinase</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Inhibit proteolytic cleavage of T3 and T4 from <u>thyroglobulin</u> → inhibits <u>thyroid hormone</u> release<br><br>* Also decrease <u>thyroid</u> vascularity and decrease the size of the gland<br><br><br> |
| Onset | <br><br>* Slow onset of action (3–4 weeks)<br><br>* <u>Methimazole</u> has a faster onset of action and fewer side effects than <u>propylthiouracil</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Rapid onset of action (within a week)<br><br> |
| Indications | <br><br>* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u><br><br>* <u>Thyroid storm</u><br><br>* After <u>radioactive iodine</u> treatment<br><br>* Before <u>radioactive iodine</u> treatment or <u>thyroidectomy</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Pretreatment before <u>thyroid surgery</u><br><br>* Adjunctive therapy in <u>thyroid storm</u><br><br>* Adjunctive therapy in <u>hyperthyroidism</u><br><br>* Used as prophylaxis to decrease <u>radioactive iodine uptake</u> in the <u>thyroid gland</u><br><br><br> |
| Special considerations | <br><br>* <u>Thionamides</u>, which are used to treat <u>hyperthyroidism</u> in <u>Graves disease</u>, are ineffective against <u>Graves ophthalmopathy</u>, which is treated with <u>glucocorticoids</u>.<br><br>* In <u>pregnancy</u><br><br>* <u>1<sup>st</sup> trimester</u>: <u>Propylthiouracil</u> is recommended.<br><br>* 2<sup>nd</sup>/<u>3<sup>rd</sup> trimester</u>: <u>carbimazole</u> or <u>methimazole</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Contraindicated in <u>pregnancy</u><br><br> |

## Adverse effects

### <u>Thionamides</u>




* <u>Allergy</u>/hypersensitivity

* The most common side effect is a pruritic <u>rash</u> (particularly with <u>methimazole</u>)

* Rarely, severe effects such as <u>exfoliative dermatitis</u>, <u>ANCA-associated vasculitis</u> (<u>propylthiouracil</u>), polyserositis, and acute <u>arthralgia</u> occur

* If mild, switch to <u>propylthiouracil</u>; if severe, avoid <u>thioamides</u> because of the risk of cross-<u>sensitivities</u>

* Hematologic side effects

* <u>Agranulocytosis</u>

* Rare but dangerous (affects ∼ 0.5% of patients; more common in elderly and those taking high doses)

* Rapidly reversible with discontinuation of treatment

* <u>Aplastic anemia</u>

* <u>Thrombocytopenia</u>

* <u>Hepatotoxicity</u> (seen with <u>propylthiouracil</u> use)

* <u>Hepatitis</u>

* <u>Cholestatic jaundice</u>

* <u>Liver</u> failure

* <u>Teratogenicity</u>: increased risk of congenital <u>malformations</u> with <u>carbimazole</u> and <u>methimazole</u> (e.g., <u>aplasia cutis</u>)

* Other

* Diffuse <u>goiter</u>

* Impaired sense of <u>taste</u> (<u>dysgeusia</u>)





> [!TIP]
> As <u>methimazole</u> and <u>carbimazole</u> are <u>teratogenic</u>, <u>propylthiouracil</u> is recommended in the <u>first trimester</u>. After the <u>first trimester</u>, switch back to <u>carbimazole</u> or <u>methimazole</u> because of the <u>hepatotoxic</u> effects of <u>propylthiouracil</u>.




### Iodides




* Side-effects are rare and often mild.

* Oral/gastric <u>mucosal</u> irritation (e.g., <u>aphthous ulcers</u>, metallic <u>taste</u>): To avoid <u>mucosal</u> irritation, iodides should be consumed with food or diluted with fluids.

* <u>Allergy</u>/hypersensitivity: <u>rash</u>, <u>angioedema</u>; rarely, severe <u>anaphylactic</u> reactions can occur

* <u>Teratogenicity</u>: contraindicated in <u>pregnancy</u> because they can cross the <u>placental barrier</u> and cause fetal <u>goiter</u>

* Iodides delay and decrease the effects of <u>radioactive iodine</u>. They must be stopped at least a week before <u>radioactive iodine ablation</u>.
